rejected.title: The Stolen Generations
card: For many years, government policies led to many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children being removed from their families. Many were placed in institutions or with non-Indigenous families.
The removals caused deep grief and loss of family, culture and language. The people removed, and their families and communities, are known as the Stolen Generations.
In 1997, the Bringing Them Home report was released after a national inquiry. It told the stories of many people who had been removed.
The report made the removals more widely known across Australia. It helped many Australians understand the harm the policies caused.
rejected.remember: Government policies removed many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, and Bringing Them Home told their stories.

a.q: What did the Bringing Them Home report of 1997 do?
opts: Told the stories of people removed from their families
Set up the policies that removed the children
Gave Aboriginal people the right to vote
Counted Aboriginal people in the census
a.why: The report came after a national inquiry and told the stories of people who had been removed. It did not create the removal policies, which came earlier, and it was not about voting or the census.
a.clue: The report came after the removals, not before.

b.q: Leila learns that her grandmother was removed from her family as a child under a government policy. Which term describes people with this experience?
opts: The Stolen Generations
The Freedom Riders
The Day of Mourning
The civil rights movement
b.why: People removed from their families under government policies, along with their families and communities, are known as the Stolen Generations. The other terms name different events or movements.
b.clue: Look for the name linked to the removal of children.

version.title: The Stolen Generations
card: From the late 1800s to the 1970s, government policies across Australia removed many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families.
Children were placed in institutions, such as Cootamundra Girls' Home and Kinchela Boys' Home in NSW, or with non-Indigenous families. Many were cut off from family, culture and language.
The children taken, and the families and communities they were taken from, are called the Stolen Generations. The removals caused grief and harm that still affect people today.
In 1997, after a national inquiry, the Bringing Them Home report told the stories of many people who were removed, often in their own words. It made the removals far more widely known.
version.remember: Policies took many children from their families, and Bringing Them Home made their stories widely known.

a.q: A historian wants first-hand accounts from people removed from their families as children. Which source fits best?
opts: The Bringing Them Home report of 1997
A 1950s government policy on removals
A census count of Aboriginal people
A list of homes run by the government
a.why: Bringing Them Home told the stories of many people who were removed, often in their own words, after a national inquiry. A government policy shows what officials planned, not what the children lived through.
a.clue: Which source records the stories of those removed?

b.q: Aunty May was taken from her family as a child and placed in a children's home. Why might her grandchildren say the removal still affects their family?
opts: Her loss of family, culture and language passed down
The home taught her family's language to her children
The home kept her in close touch with her own family
The harm of the removal ended when she left the home
b.why: Removal cut many children off from family, culture and language, and that loss carries on into later generations. The homes cut children off from their families rather than keeping them in touch.
b.clue: What did removal take away, and who else did that touch?
